metadata.title: Drawing Shapes with Math
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How a pixel decides if it is inside a shape
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Drawing Shapes with Math. Learn how a shader draws a circle, a ring and a cross using only math, then build a crosshair you can reshape with sliders.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. To draw a circle on screen, you might reach for a circle image. A shader does not need one. It asks every pixel a single question: are you inside the shape? All the answers together are the shape.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A function is a named block of code you can call. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. Its fragment function runs once for each pixel and sets its color. U V is a pixel's address, from zero to one across and down. A vector is a bundle of numbers. A uniform is a value your game sets from outside.

terms.meaning: a named block of code you can call
a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
runs once for each pixel the shape covers; sets its color
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down
a bundle of two to four numbers
a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one

beats.narration_text: Our goal: a crosshair with six dials, drawn by one shader on a Color Rect. No picture file sits behind it. Every piece is a rule, and each dial changes one rule. We start with the smallest rule.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Inside or Outside' (serif 40) top-left of the stage. A real Godot render of the finished crosshair in a SQUARE framed window on the cream stage; a script moves the six dials one after another, each out to 1.0 and back to its default (dot size, ring distance, ring width, then a pause at the defaults, then arm gap, arm length, arm width). At the top-left of the window a readout 'no picture file' lands as the pause begins; under the window a one-line caption defines the node the shader paints: 'Color Rect: a flat rectangle the shader paints'.

beats.narration_text: Here is the catch. The fragment function runs once for every pixel, and each run is handed its own pixel's address. So it does not draw a circle. It answers a question about itself: am I inside the circle?

shot.visual_intent: A 13-by-13 grid of outline cells centred on the stage (the pixel grid), the label 'fragment() · once per pixel' above it. One cell near the middle gets a terracotta ring and a small tag 'my address'; the tag then changes to 'inside?'. Then every cell answers at once: cells within five cells of the middle fill teal ('yes'), the rest stay empty ('no'), and a circle with a stepped edge appears out of the answers. Caption: 'yes: on · no: off'.

all cells answer at once; the teal circle forms

shot.motion_claim: One cell is handed its own address and asks 'inside?', then every cell answers yes or no at the same instant and a circle appears out of the answers.

beats.narration_text: To answer, a pixel needs two facts: its own address, U V, and where the center is. The center is at zero point five, zero point five. Our pixel sits at zero point six two, zero point six six.

shot.visual_intent: A square (the UV square) on the cream stage with an 'across · 0 to 1' axis along the top and a 'down · 0 to 1' axis down the left side, the second axis pointing DOWN. A terracotta cross at the middle labelled 'center · 0.5, 0.5'. A teal dot drops in to the lower right of the center, labelled 'this pixel · 0.62, 0.66'.

beats.narration_text: Work out its distance by hand. It is zero point one two to the right of the center, and zero point one six below. Square both, add them, take the square root: exactly zero point two.

shot.visual_intent: The square zooms to the center and the pixel; a caption defines the word: 'distance: how far apart two points are'. A right triangle is drawn between them: the horizontal leg labelled 0.12, the vertical leg labelled 0.16, the long side between center and pixel. Beside it the arithmetic types in as MathTex, line by line: 0.12² + 0.16², then = 0.0144 + 0.0256 = 0.04, then √0.04, then = 0.2. The long side takes the label 'distance 0.2' and a terracotta ring.

beats.narration_text: In a shader, that whole calculation is one function: distance. Give it the pixel's address and the center. Feed the answer into the color's alpha, how visible it is, and the middle fades out while the edges fill in.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the six-line shader, blank line and braces included; the distance line, then the color line, highlighted in turn); at right a real Godot window with the radial picture: nothing visible in the middle, more teal toward the edges. A label on the distance line glosses vec2(0.5) as the center; a label on the color line defines the new word: 'alpha: how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid'. A ring on the pixel worked by hand (0.62, 0.66) with the readout 'd = 0.2', and 'd = 0.7' near a corner; a thin 0 to 0.7 strip under the window with a marker.

beats.narration_text: Pick a radius, say zero point three. A pixel is inside when its distance is no more than the radius. Along the middle row, the distance dips to zero at the center. Everything under the line is inside.

shot.visual_intent: A plot on the cream stage: the x axis 'across the shape' from 0 to 1, the y axis 'distance from the middle' from 0 to 0.5. A V-shaped teal curve (0.5 at both ends, 0 at x = 0.5). A horizontal terracotta line at 0.3 labelled 'radius 0.3'. A grey dot starts on the V at the left end, above the line; it then rides the V to the right, turning teal under the line, and the stretch of the x axis where the V lies under the line (x from 0.2 to 0.8) lights up and is labelled 'inside'.

beats.narration_text: To turn that into a number, use step. Give it an edge and a value. It returns zero while the value is below the edge, and one once the value reaches it. A switch that flips at the edge.

shot.visual_intent: A small plot: the x axis 'value' from 0 to 0.6, the y axis 'output' from 0 to 1. A vertical terracotta line at 0.3 labelled 'edge'. A dot labelled 'value' starts left of the edge with a readout beside it. The step curve draws in two stretches: output 0 left of the edge, then output 1 from the edge on, labelled 'step(edge, x)'. The dot slides across the edge and the readout flips from 0 to 1. Caption (the glossary's wording): '0 below the edge, 1 from the edge up'.

beats.narration_text: Mind the order. With the radius first, step asks: has the distance reached the radius? Inside the circle, no: zero. Outside, yes: one. Swap them, and step asks: has the radius reached the distance? Inside, yes: one. That's our circle.

shot.visual_intent: A row of 25 pixel cells with centres at x = 0.02, 0.06, ... 0.98 (cells 5 to 19, the ones within 0.3 of the middle, are inside; no cell lies exactly on 0.3) with the V profile above it and the radius line. Below, a row of 0 and 1 values. First the label 'step(0.3, d)' and the small question 'd ≥ radius?': inside cells read 0 (empty), outside cells read 1 (teal), a hole. Then the two inputs trade places in the label to 'step(d, 0.3)', the question becomes 'radius ≥ d?' and the row flips: inside cells read 1 (teal), outside cells 0 (empty). Cells are numbered from 0. A terracotta ring marks cell 17, a pixel at distance 0.2 like ours (our own pixel is off this row), throughout. At the end the teal stretch is labelled 'the circle'.

beats.narration_text: Put it together. Our pixel: distance zero point two, radius zero point three, so step says one: inside. A pixel at distance zero point four says zero: outside. Those ones and zeros are a mask: how much to show.

A ring on our pixel (0.62, 0.66, inside) with the readout 'step: 1', then a ring on a pixel at distance 0.4 (0.5, 0.9, outside) with 'step: 0'; the caption defines the new word in the glossary's wording: 'mask: a number from 0 to 1 per pixel saying how much of something to show'.

beats.narration_text: A ring is a big circle with a smaller circle taken out. Draw the big mask, draw the small mask, and subtract. Where both say one, one minus one leaves zero. Only the strip between them survives.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Rings and Cutouts' (serif 40) top-left. A big teal disc labelled 'outer mask'. A smaller teal disc labelled 'inner mask' hovers above it with a minus sign between them. The small disc drops onto the big disc's center and cuts: the middle turns empty (the stage color), leaving a ring labelled 'ring'. Two number tags, set beside the shapes on leader lines and never on a fill: '1 − 1 = 0' by the hole and '1 − 0 = 1' by the band.

beats.narration_text: Now overlap two circles and add their masks. Where they overlap, both say one, so the sum is two. In a default project the screen cannot tell: an alpha of two looks exactly like one. The mistake hides.

One ring marks that stretch, then a smaller ring marks where the spot should be. A readout just below the ring (at the foot of the bite, under the spot's place) reads 'mask −1' and then 'mask 0'; 'spot: missing' lands at the top-left of the window.

beats.narration_text: The fix is max, min's mirror: it keeps the larger number. Max of minus one and zero is zero, and then the spot adds one. The rule for both bugs: after adding, cap at one; after subtracting, floor at zero.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A shape is a question each pixel answers: inside is one, outside is zero. Distance from a point, compared with a radius by step, draws a circle. Subtract masks for a ring. After adding, cap at one; after subtracting, floor at zero. Distance from a line, folded with abs, draws a band; max joins masks and multiply intersects them. Put each shape in a function, and give every slider a range of zero to one. A crosshair is a dot, a ring and four arms, joined with max.
